content_config.text: 6.1 Principles — How to Localise at the Elbow

content_config.body: The elbow is the second commonest site of nerve entrapment in the body after the wrist. Three nerves cross it, each through a predictable series of fibrous tunnels. Localisation is not guesswork: it follows from where each nerve branches.

content_config.text: 6.1.1 The three rules

content_config.body:
• Rule 1 — Branch order decides what is spared A lesion spares everything supplied proximal to it and affects everything distal.
  • So the muscle that is normal localises the lesion just as powerfully as the muscle that is weak.
  • Three examples carry most of the diagnostic weight at the elbow: brachioradialis and ECRL for the radial nerve, pronator teres for the median, and flexor carpi ulnaris for the ulnar.

• Rule 2 — Cutaneous branches that leave early are the discriminators If a sensory branch leaves proximal to a tunnel, it is spared by a lesion in that tunnel.
  • Median palmar cutaneous branch separates a proximal median lesion from carpal tunnel syndrome.
  • Ulnar dorsal cutaneous branch separates a cubital tunnel lesion from a lesion in Guyon’s canal.
  • Absent sensory loss altogether points to a purely motor nerve — the anterior interosseous or the posterior interosseous.

• Rule 3 — The dorsal root ganglion separates root from nerve A lesion proximal to the ganglion (a radiculopathy) spares the sensory nerve action potential, because the sensory cell body and its peripheral axon remain intact.
  • A lesion distal to it (plexus or peripheral nerve) reduces or abolishes the SNAP.
  • So numbness with a normal SNAP means the problem is at the root.

content_config.text: 6.1.2 The four nerves at the elbow

rows: Anteriorly, medial to the brachial artery and biceps tendon
Pronation and wrist/finger flexion (below the joint)
Posterior to the medial epicondyle — the only nerve behind the joint axis
No branches in the arm; FCU and ulnar FDP below
Elbow extension (above), brachioradialis and wrist/finger extension
Anteriorly, ending as the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve

content_config.label: Memory aid
content_config.text: A simple orientation: the ulnar nerve is the only one that passes behind the axis of flexion. That single fact explains why it — and only it — is stretched and compressed by elbow flexion, and why flexion-avoidance is the treatment.
6.2 The Median Nerve
6.2.1 Origin and course

content_config.body:
• Roots C6–T1, formed from the lateral and medial cords of the brachial plexus.
  • Descends the arm medial to the brachial artery, giving no branches in the arm.
  • Enters the cubital fossa medial to the brachial artery and the biceps tendon — the "N" of the lateral-to-medial sequence Tendon, Artery, Nerve.
  • Passes deep to the lacertus fibrosus (bicipital aponeurosis).
  • Passes between the two heads of pronator teres — the humeral head superficial, the ulnar head deep.
  • Passes beneath the fibrous arch of flexor digitorum superficialis (the "sublimis bridge") into the forearm.

content_config.text: 6.2.2 Motor supply at and below the elbow

rows: Pronator teres · flexor carpi radialis · palmaris longus · flexor digitorum superficialis
Anterior interosseous nerve (branches 5–8 cm distal to the epicondyles)
Flexor pollicis longus · flexor digitorum profundus to index and middle · pronator quadratus

content_config.text: 6.2.3 Sensory supply

content_config.body:
• Palmar cutaneous branch — arises about 5 cm proximal to the wrist crease and passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum. It supplies the skin of the thenar eminence and the central palm.
  • Digital branches — the palmar surface of the radial three and a half digits, and their dorsal tips.
  • The anterior interosseous nerve has no cutaneous territory at all — it carries only motor fibres and deep articular afferents.

content_config.text: 6.2.4 Compression sites, proximal to distal

rows: A fibrous band from a supracondylar process (a bony spur ~5 cm above the medial epicondyle, present in ~1%) to the medial epicondyle
Median symptoms; may also compress the brachial artery, so check the pulse with the elbow extended and supinated. Look for the spur on radiograph
The bicipital aponeurosis crossing the nerve
Pain reproduced by resisted elbow flexion with the forearm supinated
3. Between the heads of pronator teres
Pain reproduced by resisted pronation with the elbow extended
The fibrous proximal edge of flexor digitorum superficialis
Pain reproduced by resisted flexion of the middle finger PIP joint

content_config.text: 6.2.5 The two syndromes

content_config.body:
• Pronator syndrome Aching, fatiguing volar forearm pain, worse with repetitive pronation or gripping.
  • Sensory disturbance in the median distribution including the thenar eminence.
  • Weakness is usually mild or absent; the presentation is dominated by pain.
  • Night symptoms are uncommon, in contrast to carpal tunnel syndrome, and Phalen and Tinel at the wrist are negative.

• Anterior interosseous nerve syndrome Purely motor. Weak flexor pollicis longus and FDP to the index finger.
  • The patient cannot make a round "OK" sign — the pinch collapses into a flat, square shape because the terminal joints will not flex.
  • Pronator quadratus weakness is detected by testing resisted pronation with the elbow fully flexed (which neutralises pronator teres).
  • No sensory loss whatsoever.

content_config.label: EMG / electrodiagnostics
content_config.text:
The palmar cutaneous branch is the discriminator between a proximal median lesion and carpal tunnel syndrome. It leaves ~5 cm above the wrist and runs over the retinaculum, so it is spared in CTS but involved proximally.

Numbness including the thenar skin → lesion is proximal.

Numbness in the radial three and a half digits with a normal thenar patch → carpal tunnel.

A caution on pronator teres. Compression between its two heads is distal to the branch that supplies it, so pronator teres can be entirely normal on EMG in pronator syndrome. A normal pronator teres does not exclude a proximal median lesion — examine FCR and FDS as well.

Do not accept "AIN syndrome" at face value. A substantial proportion of cases are neuralgic amyotrophy (Parsonage–Turner) presenting with an AIN-predominant pattern. The clue is severe pain preceding the weakness by days, and subtle findings outside the AIN territory. Look for it before anyone offers a decompression.

content_config.label: Ultrasound & injection
content_config.text:
Scan the median nerve in short axis, tracing it distally from the cubital fossa. Follow it between the pronator teres heads and under the FDS arch, comparing cross-sectional area with the contralateral side.

Look specifically for a supracondylar process on the anteromedial humerus if symptoms are proximal — it is easily seen on ultrasound and easily missed on a standard radiograph.
6.3 The Ulnar Nerve

content_config.body: The nerve that defines the elbow. It is the only one passing behind the axis of flexion, and every clinical feature of cubital tunnel syndrome follows from that.

content_config.text: 6.3.1 Origin and course

content_config.body:
• Roots C8–T1, the terminal continuation of the medial cord.
  • Runs down the medial arm anterior to the medial intermuscular septum, then pierces the septum about 8 cm above the medial epicondyle to enter the posterior compartment.
  • Passes behind the medial epicondyle in the retrocondylar (ulnar) groove, where it is subcutaneous and directly palpable — the "funny bone".
  • Enters the cubital tunnel, roofed by Osborne’s ligament (the cubital tunnel retinaculum) spanning the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris.
  • Passes between the humeral and ulnar heads of FCU, then beneath the deep flexor–pronator aponeurosis into the forearm.
  • It gives no branches in the arm.

content_config.text: 6.3.2 Motor and sensory supply

content_config.body:
• Motor below the elbow: flexor carpi ulnaris and the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus (ring and little fingers). Everything else is in the hand.
  • Dorsal cutaneous branch — arises 5–8 cm proximal to the wrist, supplying the dorsum of the ulnar hand and the dorsal ulnar one and a half digits.
  • Palmar cutaneous branch — arises in the mid-forearm, supplying the skin over the hypothenar eminence.
  • Digital branches — the palmar ulnar one and a half digits.

content_config.text: 6.3.3 Why elbow flexion is the whole problem

content_config.body:
• The cubital tunnel is not a rigid tube. On flexion the retinaculum tightens and the tunnel flattens: volume falls by roughly 50–55%.
  • The nerve simultaneously elongates about 5 mm for every 45° of flexion, because it lies posterior to the axis of rotation.
  • So it is stretched and compressed at the same time. Intraneural pressure rises several-fold in full flexion, and rises further with the shoulder abducted — the sleeping posture that wakes these patients at night.

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
This anatomy is the treatment. First-line management of cubital tunnel syndrome is not surgery and not medication. It is:

Night splinting at 30–45° of extension, which prevents the sustained flexion that both compresses and stretches the nerve;

Activity modification — avoiding sustained flexion (phone use, sleeping curled up) and, critically, leaning on the elbow, which compresses a subcutaneous nerve directly against bone;

Nerve gliding exercises, performed gently and never into symptoms.

Explain the mechanism in one sentence — "bending your elbow squeezes and stretches the nerve at the same time" — and adherence improves dramatically.
6.3.4 Compression sites, proximal to distal

rows: A fascial band ~8 cm above the medial epicondyle, from the medial head of triceps to the intermuscular septum
Where the nerve pierces it; a sharp fascial edge
The bony groove itself — shallow groove, osteophytes, cubitus valgus, direct pressure
The cubital tunnel retinaculum between the two FCU heads — the classic site
The exit from the FCU, 4–5 cm distal to the epicondyle

content_config.text: 6.3.5 Clinical picture and grading

content_config.body:
• Sensory first: numbness and paraesthesia of the little and ring fingers, often nocturnal, provoked by sustained flexion.
  • Then motor: weak grip and pinch, clumsiness, and in advanced disease intrinsic wasting with a first dorsal interosseous hollow and clawing of the ring and little fingers.
  • McGowan grading — I: sensory only. II: sensory plus weakness without wasting. III: wasting and marked weakness. Grade III recovers poorly, so do not delay in a patient with visible wasting.
  • Froment’s sign (thumb IP flexion substituting for a weak adductor pollicis) and Wartenberg’s sign (little finger abduction) indicate established intrinsic weakness.

content_config.label: Pitfall — do not miss
content_config.text:
Ulnar nerve subluxation over the medial epicondyle on flexion occurs in up to 20% of asymptomatic people. Palpate for it dynamically before attributing symptoms to it, and always document it before surgery is planned, because it changes the operation.

Tardy ulnar nerve palsy appears years or decades after a childhood lateral condyle fracture that healed in cubitus valgus, which progressively stretches the nerve. In any adult with an unexplained ulnar neuropathy, measure the carrying angle and ask about childhood elbow fracture.

A snapping medial head of triceps can mimic subluxation and cause the same symptoms. Both produce a palpable clunk at the medial epicondyle on flexion; ultrasound distinguishes them.

content_config.label: EMG / electrodiagnostics
content_config.text:
The dorsal cutaneous branch localises the lesion. It leaves the ulnar nerve well proximal to Guyon’s canal, so:

Sensory loss over the dorsum of the ulnar hand → lesion at or above the forearm — cubital tunnel.

Sensory loss confined to the palmar ulnar digits with a normal dorsum → lesion at the wrist — Guyon’s canal.

Technique determines the answer. Study the nerve with the elbow flexed 70–90° and measure a 10 cm segment across the elbow. With the elbow extended the nerve lies slack in a curved path, so the surface distance underestimates the true nerve length and produces a falsely slow velocity.

Diagnostic findings: a velocity drop of >10 m/s across the elbow compared with the forearm segment, or conduction block / significant amplitude drop across the elbow. Short-segment incremental studies ("inching") localise it most precisely.

Two traps. First, FCU is frequently spared even in a genuine cubital tunnel lesion, because of fascicular topography — a normal FCU does not exclude the diagnosis. Second, a Martin–Gruber anastomosis (median-to-ulnar crossover in the forearm, in 15–20% of people) can mimic a conduction block at the elbow; consider it before reporting one.

content_config.label: Ultrasound & injection
content_config.text:
Scan in short axis in the retrocondylar groove, then above and below. A cross-sectional area above ~10–11 mm² supports the diagnosis, and the site of maximal enlargement localises the lesion.

Always scan dynamically through flexion to detect subluxation of the nerve or snapping of the medial triceps head — information that no nerve conduction study will give you.

Look for a space-occupying cause: ganglion, osteophyte, accessory anconeus epitrochlearis muscle (present in ~10–25% and a recognised cause of compression).
6.4 The Radial Nerve
6.4.1 Origin and course

content_config.body:
• Roots C5–T1 (functionally C6–C8), the largest terminal branch of the posterior cord.
  • Spirals down the posterior humerus in the spiral (radial) groove, supplying the triceps.
  • Pierces the lateral intermuscular septum about 10 cm above the lateral epicondyle to enter the anterior compartment — a fixed point, and therefore a site of tethering.
  • Lies in the groove between brachialis medially and brachioradialis laterally, anterior to the lateral epicondyle.
  • Divides at about the level of the radiocapitellar joint into two terminal branches:
  • — the superficial radial nerve — purely sensory, running under brachioradialis to the dorsoradial hand;
  • — the posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) — purely motor, passing into the supinator beneath the arcade of Frohse.

content_config.text: 6.4.2 Motor supply, in branch order

rows: Spared in any lesion below the groove
Brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis longus, part of brachialis
The two key discriminator muscles. Both are spared in a PIN lesion
Supinator · ECRB (variable) · EDC · EDM · ECU · APL · EPB · EPL · EIP
All lost in a PIN lesion
Its sparing is what makes PIN lesions painless and numbness-free

content_config.label: Memory aid
content_config.text: Brachioradialis is a flexor supplied by the radial nerve, and it is C5–C6. That makes it doubly useful: it separates a radial neuropathy from a C6 radiculopathy, and it separates a spiral groove lesion from a PIN lesion.
6.4.3 Sensory supply

content_config.body:
• Posterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm — given off in the arm, so it is spared by everything at or below the elbow.
  • Superficial radial nerve — the dorsoradial hand and the first dorsal web space, the classic "anatomical snuffbox" patch.
  • The PIN carries no cutaneous fibres — only motor and deep articular afferents to the posterolateral capsule and the radiocapitellar joint.

content_config.text: 6.4.4 The radial tunnel — five potential compression points

content_config.body:
• Fibrous bands anterior to the radiocapitellar joint
  • The leash of Henry — the radial recurrent vessels crossing the nerve
  • The medial (sharp tendinous) edge of ECRB
  • The arcade of Frohse — the fibrous proximal edge of supinator; the commonest site
  • The distal edge of supinator

content_config.text: 6.4.5 The two syndromes — the same tunnel, different presentations

rows: None — the PIN is purely motor
Present but deviates radially — ECRL is spared, ECU is not
3–5 cm distal to the lateral epicondyle, over the supinator
Resisted supination with the elbow extended; resisted middle finger extension

content_config.label: Pitfall — do not miss
content_config.text:
Radial tunnel syndrome is the great mimic of tennis elbow, and the commonest reason a "tennis elbow" fails to settle. Both produce lateral elbow pain in the same patient population.

The discriminator is where you press. Lateral epicondylalgia is tender at the ECRB origin, just distal and anterior to the epicondyle tip. Radial tunnel syndrome is tender 3–5 cm further distal, over the supinator mass.

They coexist in perhaps 5–10% of resistant cases, which is why a patient can improve partially after treatment for one and remain symptomatic from the other.

content_config.label: EMG / electrodiagnostics
content_config.text:
The single most useful radial rule at the elbow. A patient with finger drop, a wrist that still extends but drifts radially, and entirely normal sensation has a PIN lesion — not a spiral groove palsy and not a C7 radiculopathy.

Add brachioradialis and ECRL to the needle study. Both are radial but supplied proximal to the PIN:

Abnormal brachioradialis + wrist drop + sensory loss in the dorsal web space → lesion at the spiral groove ("Saturday night palsy"). Triceps is usually spared because its branches leave above the groove.

Normal brachioradialis and ECRL + finger drop + no sensory loss → PIN lesion.

Weak brachioradialis with a reduced lateral antebrachial SNAP and neck pain → think C6 radiculopathy and check the paraspinals.

Remember that radial tunnel syndrome is a clinical diagnosis. Normal electrodiagnosis does not exclude it, because pain-fibre compression without axonal loss produces no abnormality on standard studies.

content_config.label: Ultrasound & injection
content_config.text:
Follow the radial nerve in short axis from the lateral supracondylar region down to its division at the radiocapitellar joint, then track the PIN into and through the supinator.

Look for a thickened arcade of Frohse, nerve enlargement at the supinator entry, or a ganglion arising from the radiocapitellar joint — a recognised and surgically correctable cause of PIN palsy that electrodiagnosis alone will not reveal.
6.5 Cutaneous Nerves Around the Elbow

rows: Terminal branch of the musculocutaneous nerve; emerges lateral to the biceps tendon
The nerve injured in distal biceps tendon repair, and in awkward antecubital venepuncture. Its SNAP is also the standard study for the lateral cord and C6
Medial cord (C8–T1) directly — it never enters the ulnar nerve
Its SNAP is reduced in lower trunk plexopathy and true neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome, but normal in ulnar neuropathy at the elbow — a crucial separation
Spared in all lesions at or below the elbow; affected in high radial lesions

content_config.label: EMG / electrodiagnostics
content_config.text:
The medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve is the most under-used study in the upper limb. Because it leaves the medial cord before the ulnar nerve forms, it is:

Normal in ulnar neuropathy at the elbow or wrist;

Abnormal in a lower trunk or medial cord plexopathy and in true neurogenic TOS.

So in a patient with ulnar-distribution numbness and equivocal ulnar conduction studies, the MABC response tells you whether the problem is actually above the elbow.
6.6 Innervation of the Joint Itself

content_config.body: Frequently omitted from teaching, and the reason several elbow presentations are hard to localise. Hilton’s law applies: the nerve supplying a muscle crossing a joint also supplies the joint and the skin over it. Since four nerves cross the elbow, all four contribute articular branches.

content_config.text: 6.6.1 By quadrant

rows: Ulnar — branches given off as it passes the retrocondylar groove, supplying the medial collateral ligament and posteromedial capsule
Radial, largely through the posterior interosseous nerve and the nerve to anconeus

content_config.body:
• The anterior capsule is the most densely innervated region, and the capsule as a whole is rich in both nociceptors and mechanoreceptors.
  • The overlying skin follows the same nerves: lateral antebrachial cutaneous laterally, medial antebrachial cutaneous medially, posterior antebrachial cutaneous posteriorly.

content_config.text: 6.6.2 Four clinical consequences

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
1. Medial elbow pain is anatomically ambiguous. The ulnar nerve gives its articular branches at exactly the point where it is most often compressed. So joint, ligament and nerve are inseparable there — which is why medial epicondylalgia, UCL injury and cubital tunnel syndrome coexist so often, and why every patient with medial epicondylalgia needs an ulnar nerve examination.

2. Posterolateral pain may be neural. The PIN supplies the posterolateral capsule and the radiocapitellar joint. That articular afferent load contributes to the deep, poorly localised ache of radial tunnel syndrome — pain without weakness, arising from a nerve carrying joint sensation.

3. Capsular afferents drive stiffness. A distended, painful capsule reflexively inhibits the surrounding muscles and the patient splints at 70–80°, the position of maximum capsular volume. Combined with brachialis lying directly on the anterior capsule, this is a large part of why the elbow stiffens so readily after trauma.

4. Denervation is possible but immature. Because the supply is spread across four quadrants, surgical denervation (the Wilhelm technique) must address several branches. Percutaneous articular-branch blocks and radiofrequency for painful elbow arthritis are described, but the evidence base is far thinner than for the genicular nerves at the knee, and cadaveric branch patterns vary considerably between individuals. Know that it exists; do not present it as standard care.
6.7 Putting It Together
6.7.1 The localisation table
6.7.2 A bedside sequence for the weak or painful elbow

content_config.body:
• Inspect — muscle bulk (first dorsal interosseous, thenar, forearm), carrying angle, scars, and the position the patient holds the elbow in.
  • Test the three discriminator muscles: brachioradialis (radial, above the PIN), pronator teres and FCR (median), FCU and first dorsal interosseous (ulnar).
  • Map the sensation in four patches: thenar eminence, dorsal web space, dorsum of the ulnar hand, lateral forearm. These four separate almost every lesion at this level.
  • Palpate and roll the ulnar nerve in the retrocondylar groove, and flex the elbow fully to check for subluxation.
  • Press two points laterally: the ECRB origin at the epicondyle, and the supinator 3–5 cm distal. They separate tennis elbow from radial tunnel.
  • Provocative tests as indicated — resisted pronation, resisted middle finger PIP flexion, resisted middle finger extension, resisted supination, elbow flexion test.
  • Then decide whether electrodiagnosis will answer the question, and which muscles will answer it.

content_config.text: 6.7.3 Ten things to carry into clinic

content_config.body:
• The ulnar nerve is the only one passing behind the flexion axis — which is why flexion both compresses and stretches it, and why extension splinting works.
  • Cubital tunnel volume falls ~50–55% on flexion, and the nerve elongates ~5 mm per 45°.
  • The dorsal cutaneous branch separates cubital tunnel from Guyon’s canal — dorsal ulnar numbness means the elbow.
  • FCU is often spared in a genuine cubital tunnel lesion. A normal FCU does not exclude the diagnosis.
  • Study the ulnar nerve at 70–90° of flexion over a 10 cm segment, or you will manufacture a false slowing.
  • The palmar cutaneous branch separates pronator syndrome from carpal tunnel syndrome — thenar numbness means proximal.
  • Pronator teres may be normal in pronator syndrome, because compression is distal to its branch.
  • PIN is purely motor; radial tunnel syndrome is pure pain. Weakness with normal sensation localises instantly.
  • ECRL is supplied above the PIN, so the wrist still extends in PIN palsy — but drifts radially.
  • All four nerves supply the joint itself, which is why medial elbow pain is so often joint, ligament and nerve together.
